results.title: CoreWeave, Nebius Surge as AI GPU Rentals Undercut Big Tech Clouds - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights:
CoreWeave and Nebius Group, emerging powers in artificial intelligence infrastructure, are drawing attention after posting second-quarter results that beat market expectations. Unlike full-service cloud providers such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google, so-called neoclouds are built around Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) and specialize in delivering faster, cheaper infrastructure for AI computing.

...

Neoclouds are companies that rent or sell GPU-centered cloud capacity tailored to AI training and inference. Their scope is narrower than that of established cloud providers, which use both central processing units (CPUs) and GPUs to deliver general-purpose services such as storage, databases and web services all at once. In exchange, they let customers quickly rent GPU infrastructure at prices up to 66% lower than those of the large incumbent cloud providers. So far this year, share-price returns at the three major cloud players — Google, Microsoft and Amazon — have lagged amid concerns about the risks of their vast investments and businesses, while neoclouds have held up relatively well.

results.title: AI Cloud Prices Rise by 25%, Intensifying Platform Competition | WEEX Crypto News
highlights:
On the afternoon of the 13th at 3:58 PM (Korean time), analyst qinbafrank posted an analysis on X, stating that the recent performances of CoreWeave and Nebius demonstrate the rapid expansion phase of the AI cloud service provider industry. However, since this analysis was presented by a media outlet, it is necessary to read it separately from the figures disclosed by each company in their public announcements and shareholder letters.

A common point revealed in the performances of both companies is the shortage of AI computing supply. The analysis indicated that Nebius's average annual revenue from new contracts in the second quarter exceeded $20 million per MW (approximately 2.83 billion KRW), with some projects reaching between $20 million and $25 million per MW.

The price increase is not a uniform trend across all GPU resources. According to the analysis reported by O'Daily, CoreWeave's GPU computing SKU prices rose by about 25% in July, while Nebius's prices for older generation GPUs increased by over 30% compared to the first quarter. The price for short-term emergency capacity was reported to be between $40 million and $50 million per MW (approximately 5.67 billion to 7.09 billion KRW).

The price reevaluation is first appearing in high-value resources that can be deployed immediately, such as short-term capacity, new generation GPUs, large clusters, and production AI inference. In contrast, existing computing resources that are lower in priority or locked in at long-term fixed prices find it difficult to reflect the same level of price increase.

results.title: The H100 is getting an exchange-traded futures contract. Yet the H100 itself still has no single price: $2.74 or $7.20 for the same GPU-hour. | Illia Martyn
highlights:
# The H100 is getting an exchange-traded futures contract. Yet the H100 itself still has no single price: $2.74 or $7.20 for the same GPU-hour. | Illia Martyn · LinkedIn · 2026-08-13T00:00:00+00:00

...

The H100 is getting an exchange-traded futures contract. Yet the H100 itself still has no single price: $2.74 or $7.20 for the same GPU-hour.

CME plans to launch trading on October 5, 2026, subject to regulatory review. Separate futures will track the rental cost of Nvidia H100 and B200 GPUs. This isn't about buying and delivering graphics cards: one contract represents one month of renting one GPU, with cash settlement.

The point is quite practical. A company that will need computing power in six months can hedge against rising rental prices. A data center can hedge against falling prices. All through a commodity exchange familiar to big business, with centralized clearing, rather than an agreement scribbled on a napkin between two cloud providers.

Public prices and expectations for future prices already exist. Silicon Data publishes daily indexes and calculates a forward curve based on actual rental agreements, while contracts on the future cost of GPU compute have been trading on Kalshi since July. What's new about CME is the standard regulated futures contract—a format that corporations can more easily integrate into risk management.

But compute is still far from becoming a true exchange-traded commodity. On August 12, an H100-hour cost $2.74 from neoclouds and $7.20 from hyperscalers. That's a 2.6-fold difference due to configuration, rental term, platform, and geography.

GPUs are called the new oil. For now, it's oil whose price depends on the exact bucket it came in.

results.title: Nvidia AI Infrastructure Financing Under Falling GPU Rental Prices: Implications for Nvidia, AI Clouds, and Customers – aitechmodel.com
highlights:
## Are GPU rental prices actually falling?

The evidence shows a segmented market rather than a broad current decline. Nvidia said H100 rental prices had risen 20% year to date by May 2026, while A100 cloud pricing had increased nearly 15%, according to its May earnings call. Independent benchmarks show wide differences by provider and chip. On August 12, Silicon data put H100 on-demand pricing at $2.74 an hour among neocloud s, specialized GPU-cloud providers, versus $7.20 at hyperscalers. Its benchmark also showed H200 pricing falling 0.6% over seven days in a market split by provider, contract, specification, and location.

A prior decline is well documented. JPMorgan Asset Management found that most neocloud and hyperscaler GPU rates fell 20% to 25% through December 2025. H100 neocloud rates dropped from $2.70 to $2.00 an hour. The useful distinction is between historical repricing and current market-wide direction. Some chips, regions, and contract types can become cheaper while scarce or heavily demanded capacity becomes more expensive.

...

nvidia announced memorandums with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure. The stated purpose is to broaden access to computing capacity and support hardware sales and software adoption, but the agreements remained prospective as of August 10. ... A memorandum is not an executed financing agreement, and mobilizable capital is not booked Nvidia revenue. Nvidia benefits only when funded projects proceed and translate into purchases or adoption.

...

Customers should not treat "the GPU price" as a single market number. The $2.74 neocloud and $7.20 hyperscaler H100 benchmarks compare broad provider groups, not necessarily identical services or workload outcomes. For a defensible comparison, request quotes that match on: A lower hourly rate may not produce a lower workload cost if jobs run more slowly or the needed capacity is unavailable.

Conversely, specialized providers may offer meaningful savings when their performance and contract terms meet the same requirements. Customers with flexible timing can compare short-term pricing against committed rates. Buyers with steady demand should test whether a longer agreement reduces cost enough to justify the risk of later market declines.

- GPU model, memory, and other relevant specifications
- On-demand or committed contract term
- Deployment location
- Measured platform performance for the intended workload
- Capacity availability during the required period

results.title: A GPU Hour Is Not a Barrel of Oil – Jason A. Hoffman
highlights:
The latest version is more concrete. CME Group and Silicon Data plan to launch two cash-settled futures contracts on October 5, pending regulatory review, tied to benchmark rental prices for NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs. Other firms are developing compute futures, exchanges, and exchange-for-physical mechanisms. The stated ambition is to make GPU capacity easier to price, finance, reserve, and trade.

...

There are real reasons a GPU rental contract may work better than a generalized cloud-compute contract.

First, the device has a recognizable identity. An NVIDIA H100 or B200 is a named product with published specifications. Buyers understand the broad performance generation they are requesting, and suppliers often own the same underlying hardware.

Second, the market has experienced actual scarcity and visible price volatility. GPU owners, neoclouds, model developers, enterprises, and financial counterparties have exposure to changes in capacity prices. That creates a more credible population of natural hedgers than existed for a generic unit of cloud compute.

Third, the equipment is capital intensive, but it does not follow one depreciation curve. Book value, resale value, rental revenue, physical condition, and frontier suitability move on different clocks. A new generation can reduce an older GPU’s earning power for frontier workloads even while the device remains physically sound, scarce, and valuable elsewhere. Owners want utilization and revenue visibility. Buyers want budget and capacity visibility. Lenders and investors want a reference price that can help them model residual value, contracted revenue, and downside cases.

...

The honest description, however, is narrower. An H100 rental-price future is a financial hedge against a defined H100 rental-price benchmark. It may help a buyer or seller reduce exposure to broad movements in rental rates. It does not guarantee that the buyer can obtain the right cluster, in the right location, with the right topology, software, service level, and delivery date. It also does not make capacity from every constituent provider operationally interchangeable.

...

Fast product turnover adds another complication. A contract family tied to a specific GPU generation must remain liquid even as demand for that vintage changes composition and migrates among workload classes and providers. Rolling from H100 to B200 and then to later architectures is not analogous to updating the sulfur specification for a durable commodity. Each generation can change system design, cooling, networking, software, performance, and relative economics. A continuous “compute” index may conceal both the discontinuities between new systems and the continuing value of older ones in other markets.

# Zettabyte launches Model-as-a-Service on zCLOUD

The service provides API access to open-source models running on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPUs.

Zettabyte announced the general availability of Model-as-a-Service on zCLOUD, its GPU cloud. Teams can efficiently call open-source models through API on Zettabyte’s NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPUs.

### Model-as-a-Service

With Model-as-a-Service, zCLOUD hosts popular open weight and open-source models, ready to call through an API and run on Zettabyte’s GPUs. Teams can build on them directly, without sourcing, installing, and tuning a model themselves. Teams that want raw capacity can still rent GPUs on zCLOUD and run their own models.

### GPU availability

NVIDIA H100 is available today, with pricing from US$1.99 per GPU-hour depending on needs and scale. zCLOUD is backed by a 99.5 percent uptime SLA target, and reserved clusters are built to deploy in under six hours from confirmed requirements.

### Ways to access GPU capacity

Zettabyte offers three ways to access capacity:

- Short-Term Capacity – GPU instances that scale to hundreds of GPUs, with no long-term commitment.
- Reserved Clusters – Predictable, fully managed capacity for sustained training and inference under a term commitment.
- Private Cloud – Custom deployments for teams with procurement, security, or region requirements.
